Code side for the VPS is pushed (dd30a3a). Caddy's ask is GET /.well-known/spirit-name?domain=<host> on puppetPost's port, answered only when Host is 127.0.0.1/localhost[:port]: 200 when the owner names a key for it, 404 otherwise. So the global block is on_demand_tls { ask http://127.0.0.1:<face port>/.well-known/spirit-name }, with tls { on_demand } on face.spirit.<domain> and *.face.spirit.<domain>. The new-name budget is 20/min, shared with visits. Andy also said go (again) and wants to be told when spirit-3 is ready for him to SSH in. When your scripts are in, tell me and I'll give him the exact commands to run: the VPS part, plus face-domain.json and join's grant row on his box.

READY for you to SSH into spirit-3 (scripts pushed at efa5a3a; the full runbook is bash/FACE.md). Bring two things from your node: your node's public key (MCow...), and an invite for 'face' minted on your relay (Natter, the relay's panel, as for any member). On spirit-3 as root: (1) cd /root/SpiritOS && ./bash/update, to get the scripts. (2) /root/SpiritOS/bash/face-install <YOUR_NODE_KEY> <INVITE>. It prints the face node's key at the end, and may stop asking you to add a 4-line block to the top of /etc/caddy/Caddyfile; FACE.md step 3 has it. Then on YOUR node: accept the face node's key as a contact, and put face-domain.json and grants.json into spirit/run/app/appFaceApp/ (FACE.md step 4 has both). Then: curl -sS https://join.face.spirit.andyflinn.com/ should give 501 last-leg-not-built with your key, which proves the route. Honest caveat: I tested the scripts' syntax, and a real face node locally, but not the root/systemd/Caddy parts; spirit-3 is their first run, so paste me anything that goes red.
taking public-app-server/G17 -- Andy's 'the install claims an invite' note.

Good, and it closes a real gap: today nothing in the tree writes puppet.json, so a puppet is bound to its owner by someone typing the owner's key into a file on the VPS. The invite way, as with the relay's first claim: (1) your box mints a one-time PUPPET invite. (2) The VPS install is given that invite and claims it: a packet to your box with the invite, signed by the VPS's own new key. (3) Your box checks the invite is its own and unspent, marks it spent, and answers with its key. (4) The VPS writes puppet.json { owner: <your key> } itself. From then on it's your puppet, and nobody typed a key. Timing is your call: (a) step 1 goes live first with puppet.json written by hand this once, and the invite claim becomes the next slice, or (b) the invite claim is built before spirit-3 goes live. Go! = (a), which gets you the browser proof sooner.
taking public-app-server/G17 -- Andy's 'the owner key is installed as well'.

Understood: the install takes your key as an argument and writes it into puppet.json on the VPS, so it's installed, not typed into a file afterwards. The invite claim then confirms the pairing from both sides: your box learns the VPS's new key and marks the invite spent. For step 1 that means the script writes puppet.json from the key you give it; the invite claim follows as its own slice. I'll pass that to wsl-claude for the scripts.

For your install script, from Andy: 'at VPS install time, the owner key is installed as well'. So the VPS install takes the owner's key as an argument and writes relay-state/puppet.json { owner: <key>, carries: [] } itself, plus face.json { port }. The invite claim (the owner mints a one-time puppet invite, the install claims it, the owner learns the VPS key) is the next slice; don't wait for it for step 1.
